title: Rent Assistance
subtitle: Search by household, housing type and urgency, not by one magic program name

blocks.text: Rent assistance has a small naming problem: the same idea may arrive as a benefit, subsidy, supplement, allowance or wait-list letter wearing sensible shoes.

Rent help in Canada comes from provinces, territories, cities, Indigenous groups and housing providers. It may be cash help that moves with you, housing where rent is set by your income, a rent top-up tied to one unit, or short-term help to stop an eviction. What is offered, who goes first and how long it takes differ by area. The right search starts with your household and your housing.
The Canada Housing Benefit is delivered through thirteen separate provincial and territorial programs. It is not one national website with one national rate.

items.title: “Anyone paying more than 30% of income on rent automatically receives a subsidy.”
items.text: Thirty percent is a common measure of what is affordable, not an approval code. Income limits, who goes first, the type of housing, funding and wait-list rules still decide who gets help.

blocks.text: CMHC: Affordable housing programs across Canada
Knowing which kind of rent help fits you keeps you from waiting in a line that was never yours.
blocks.detail: Four kinds of help look alike from the outside, and each one has its own door.
blocks.extra: Section 02 lays out the four doors.

sections.title: Four Doors Can Look Like Rent Help

blocks.text: Read the doors before you assume they all lead to the same room.

items.title: RENT HELP THAT MOVES WITH YOU
items.text: A payment that follows your household to a regular rental that qualifies, under local rules and yearly renewal.

items.title: RENT SET BY YOUR INCOME
items.text: Your rent is tied to your household income in an approved unit. Getting in often means a central or local wait list.

items.title: TOP-UP TIED TO ONE UNIT
items.text: The money is tied to a specific landlord, co-op or housing provider. Moving may end the help.

items.title: EMERGENCY HOUSING HELP
items.text: Short-term funds, income support, rent banks or prevention services may help with back rent, deposits or an urgent risk of losing your home.

blocks.text: B.C. keeps its Rental Assistance Program for working families with children separate from SAFER, which helps renters aged 60 or older. Your household type changes the door.
Alberta offers monthly rent benefits and community-based affordable housing. Local housing providers may handle the applications, so the provincial page is often the map, not the final counter.

items.title: “Joining one housing wait list places me on every relevant list.”
items.text: Cities, housing providers and special programs may each keep their own list. Ask which lists, buildings and rent benefits need a separate application.

blocks.text: Alberta: Rent assistance

sections.title: Measure the Gap Before You Choose a Door

blocks.text: Write down your household income before and after tax, your monthly rent, which utilities are included, unit size, any accessibility needs, who lives with you and any back rent. A simple way to measure the pressure is rent divided by income before tax, but use the program’s own income rules to see if you qualify.
A rent receipt proves you paid. A lease proves the terms of your tenancy. Many applications need both, plus tax information, proof of income, status papers and household details.

If rent is late or you get an eviction notice, contact your landlord or housing provider and a local tenant, legal or housing help service right away. Ask for a written plan to pay back what you owe, and apply for emergency help. A subsidy wait list is not an answer to an eviction deadline.

Rent help that moves with you may need a yearly income check and a report when you move or your household changes. Help tied to one unit may end when you leave. Read the renewal letter before you give notice to move.

items.title: “A rent subsidy solves every housing-cost problem.”
items.text: Utilities, parking, insurance, moving costs and rent above the program limit may still be yours to pay. Build a full housing budget. The lease has supporting actors.

blocks.text: Key takeaway
Finding rent help is a local matching job. Measure your housing gap, find out whether help follows you or the unit, apply to every route that fits and treat back rent as an urgent problem.

sections.title: Alicia and the Wait List That Wasn’t a Rescue Boat

blocks.text: Meet Alicia
paragraphs: Alicia Morgan rents a one-bedroom in Toronto with her son. Her goal is to stay in that apartment, close to his school. Last year she applied for community housing and got a letter saying she is on the wait list.

In March, her hours at the store are cut. She misses half of April’s rent. She figures the wait-list letter will protect her. The letter stays calm, laminated and entirely unable to negotiate with her landlord.
In May, an eviction notice slides under her door. She calls the housing office, hoping the list can speed up. The answer is no. The list could take years.

Alicia is tempted to stop answering the landlord’s calls until something changes. Instead, she decides to call a tenant clinic that same afternoon. The worker tells her that a wait list and an eviction are two different problems, and she needs a plan for both.

With the clinic’s help, she writes her landlord a plan to pay back the missed rent over four months. She gathers her lease, her rent record, her tax notice and the letter about her cut hours. She also applies for emergency rent help.
There is one more surprise. The worker asks about a rent benefit that moves with her, instead of waiting for a new unit. Alicia had never heard of it. She applies that week.
The landlord accepts the plan. Alicia keeps her apartment, her son keeps his school, and her wait-list file stays current. The laminated letter still cannot negotiate. Alicia can.

blocks.text: Update your housing applications when your phone, address, household, income or accessibility needs change. A closed file can spend years waiting perfectly in the wrong place.
Alicia kept her home by treating the eviction as its own emergency instead of waiting on the housing list.
blocks.detail: Working on today’s rent and the long-term list at the same time protects your home now and later.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is the Canada Housing Benefit not one national application?
items.detail: It is delivered through thirteen separate provincial and territorial programs, each with its own rules, website and rate.

items.title: Which four kinds of rent help should you compare?
items.detail: Rent help that moves with you, rent set by your income, a top-up tied to one unit and emergency housing help.

items.title: Which papers prove your income, your tenancy and your payments?
items.detail: Tax information and income records prove income. A lease proves the terms of your tenancy. A rent receipt or rent record proves payment.

items.title: Why should an eviction risk not wait for a subsidy list?
items.detail: A wait list deals with long-term housing over time. An eviction notice is a deadline now, so contact your landlord and find emergency help right away.

items.title: What should you check before you move out of a unit with rent help?
items.detail: Whether the help is tied to the unit, which would end when you leave, or moves with you, and what the renewal letter asks before you give notice.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Rent Assistance Search and Stability File

blocks.text: Use rounded numbers and short labels. Keep leases, notices, ID and bank details in a safe file outside this form.
Never pay an unofficial “application fee” to jump a public housing wait list. Check the agency, website and contact details before you share ID or money records.

items.title: Portable benefit
items.text: Rent help that may move with your household.

items.title: RGI
items.text: Rent-geared-to-income housing, where rent is set by your income.

items.title: Unit-based supplement
items.text: Rent help tied to one specific unit.

items.title: Housing-cost ratio
items.text: Your rent or housing cost compared with your household income.

items.title: Rent ledger
items.text: Your landlord’s record of rent charged and paid.

items.title: Wait list
items.text: A line for housing or help, under local rules about who goes first.

quiz.question: True or False: “Anyone paying more than 30% of income on rent automatically receives a subsidy.”

questions: Which city and province do you live in?
About how much is your rent, and about how much does your household earn each month? Estimates are fine.
Is your rent behind, or have you received an eviction notice? (Yes / No / Not sure)
Which rent help have you already applied for? Write “none yet” if you have not applied.
Who lives with you? Mention children, anyone 60 or older, or anyone with a disability.
What is one call you will make this week?
